title: When to Fine-Tune and When Not To

content.title: When to Fine-Tune and When Not To

blocks.text: This topic closes out the Introduction to Fine-Tuning module by pulling together everything covered so far, why fine-tuning helps, how it differs from prompting and RAG, and what kinds of fine-tuning exist, into one practical checklist for deciding whether to fine-tune at all.
The short version, fine-tuning is usually the last technique to reach for, not the first, and it pays off most clearly when a task is stable, high volume, and backed by enough quality data.
1. Revisiting the Question This Whole Module Has Been Building Toward

blocks.alt: Prompting and RAG typically come before fine-tuning in the escalation order

blocks.text: Across the earlier topics in this module, a consistent pattern emerged, prompting is fastest to iterate on, RAG solves the freshness problem, and fine-tuning solves the consistency and behavior problem, each earning its place for a different reason.
The practical question is rarely does fine-tuning work, it almost always can shift behavior to some degree, the real question is does fine-tuning earn its cost for this particular task, right now.
2. Signals That Point Toward Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: High volume, a stable task, and good data together point toward fine-tuning

blocks.text: Fine-tuning tends to pay off clearly when three conditions line up together, the request volume is high enough that per call savings matter, the task definition has stabilized rather than still shifting weekly, and there is enough good quality data available to actually train on.

blocks.title: All three matter together
blocks.content: Having only one or two of these conditions is often not enough, a stable, high volume task with poor data, or a well documented task with low volume, both weaken the case for fine-tuning.

blocks.text: 3. Signals That Point Away From Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Low volume is compared against a frequently changing task, both weakening the case for fine-tuning

blocks.text: Low request volume undercuts the cost argument for fine-tuning, since the upfront training cost may never be recovered through savings on individual calls.

A task definition that is still actively changing is an even stronger signal against fine-tuning right now, since each meaningful change would require collecting new data and retraining, while a prompt can simply be edited.
4. The Data Availability Test

blocks.alt: Not having enough quality data points toward waiting rather than fine-tuning yet

blocks.text: Before committing to fine-tuning, honestly assess whether you actually have, or can realistically collect, enough good quality examples of the exact behavior you want. Without that, training is likely to produce a model that learned noise rather than the intended pattern.
This is often the single most limiting factor in practice, teams frequently want to fine-tune before they have the data to do it well, and collecting that data becomes the real first project.
5. The Volume Test

blocks.alt: A few calls a day is compared against thousands of calls a day

blocks.text: A rough rule of thumb, if a task runs only a handful of times a day, the upfront cost of collecting data and training rarely pays back quickly enough to justify fine-tuning over a well written prompt.
As volume climbs into the thousands of calls per day range, the token savings and consistency gains from fine-tuning start to compound meaningfully, strengthening the case considerably.

blocks.text: 6. When You Genuinely Need Fresh Facts Instead

blocks.alt: Facts that change often point toward using RAG instead of fine-tuning

blocks.text: If the underlying problem is that the model does not know something current, pricing, inventory, recent events, fine-tuning is the wrong tool regardless of how well the other signals line up, since it cannot keep pace with frequently changing facts, a distinction covered in full in the earlier Fine-Tuning vs RAG topic.
7. Starting Cheap and Escalating Only When Needed

blocks.alt: Starting with prompting, adding RAG if needed, then fine-tuning last if still needed

blocks.text: A sensible default order for almost any new task is to start with prompting, since it is fastest to test and iterate on, add RAG if the gap is about missing or outdated knowledge, and only reach for fine-tuning once the task has proven stable and the remaining gap is clearly about behavior, not knowledge.
8. A Final Checklist

items: The task has a clear, stable definition that has not changed in weeks
Request volume is high enough that per call savings and consistency gains actually matter
You have, or can realistically collect, enough good quality labeled examples
The gap you are trying to close is about behavior, tone, or format, not missing current facts
You have already tried prompting seriously and it genuinely falls short on consistency or cost

blocks.text: Worked Example

A small internal tool used by five people a few times a week to draft meeting notes is a poor fine-tuning candidate, low volume, and the format keeps changing as the team experiments, prompting remains the right tool here.

A customer facing chatbot handling twenty thousand conversations a day, with a support tone that has been stable for six months and three years of historical conversation logs to learn from, is a strong fine-tuning candidate, every signal in the checklist points the same direction.
Common Mistakes

items: Fine-tuning a low volume, rarely used task where the training cost will never be recovered
Fine-tuning on a task definition that is still actively evolving, requiring repeated costly retraining
Reaching for fine-tuning to solve a freshness problem that RAG would solve far more directly
Skipping the honest data availability check and training on whatever data happens to be on hand

blocks.text: Practice

Run the final checklist in this topic against a real task you are considering fine-tuning for. Count how many boxes it genuinely checks, and if it checks fewer than three, treat that as a signal to keep improving your prompting or retrieval approach first.
Key Takeaway

Fine-tuning earns its cost when a task is stable, high volume, backed by good data, and the gap you are closing is about behavior rather than missing facts, which is why it usually belongs at the end of an escalation path that starts with prompting and adds retrieval before ever reaching for a training run.
